title: The Cost of Trusting a Fluent AI Answer
summary: Smooth AI answers feel finished before anyone checks them. Why fluency reads as truth, what the data shows it costs, and five habits that get past the polish.
author: Nguyen Le Phong
html:
Say a teammate asks an AI assistant why some customers were charged twice last night. The answer comes back in four tidy paragraphs. It names the cause (a retry after a gateway timeout), explains idempotency in the right words, suggests a one-line fix and even lists a trade-off. It reads like something a senior engineer would write. The PR goes up with that explanation pasted into the description, and the reviewer, busy and reassured, approves it.

Two weeks later it happens again. The retry was real, but the fix only covered one of the two code paths that call the gateway. Nobody checked, because the answer sounded like it had already been checked.

Why a smooth answer feels finished

When text is easy to read, we tend to treat it as more likely to be right. Clear structure, field vocabulary and a confident tone all lower the effort of reading, and lower effort feels a lot like agreement. With a person, that shortcut mostly works, because people who explain things well usually know them well.

With a language model, the link between tone and knowledge is much weaker. In September 2025, researchers from OpenAI and Georgia Tech argued that models guess when unsure and end up "producing plausible yet incorrect statements," partly because training and evaluation "reward guessing over acknowledging uncertainty" (Why Language Models Hallucinate). In plain terms: the model has been rewarded for sounding sure, so it often sounds sure even when it shouldn't. The tone tells you about the training. It tells you little about whether this particular answer is right.

Where the cost shows up

The cost is rarely a dramatic outage. It's usually smaller and easier to miss:

  • An afternoon spent fixing the wrong layer because the diagnosis read so well.
  • A fix that covers one path out of two, like the double charge above.
  • A product decision based on a summary that left out the awkward customer quotes.
  • A bit less understanding of your own system each time, because the answer did the thinking you'd normally do.

Developers feel this already. In Stack Overflow's 2025 survey, the most common frustration with AI tools, picked by 66% of respondents, was "AI solutions that are almost right, but not quite," followed by "Debugging AI-generated code is more time-consuming" at 45% (2025 Developer Survey, AI section). Almost right is exactly where fluency does the most damage. A wrong answer gets caught. An almost-right one, written well, gets merged.

The security side is sharper. In a Stanford user study published at ACM CCS 2023, participants who had an AI assistant wrote significantly less secure code than those without one, and they were more likely to believe their code was secure (Perry et al.). Quality went down while confidence went up. The same paper found that people who trusted the AI less and worked harder on their prompts ended up with fewer vulnerabilities.

The smooth-answer trap

A fluent answer makes reading easier. Your responsibility stays the same size. The more convincing an answer sounds, the more it's worth pulling out each claim and asking how you'd check it.

Habits that get past the polish

You don't need to distrust everything. You need a few habits that take the tone out of the picture so you can see what's actually being claimed.

  1. Strip it down to claims. Rewrite the answer as a short list: "the duplicate comes from a retry," "the retry happens after a gateway timeout," "this one line prevents it." Without the nice paragraphs, it's much easier to see which claims have any evidence behind them.
  2. Check the most specific detail first. Version numbers, flag names, function signatures, config keys. Specific details are where made-up content tends to hide, and they're the cheapest thing to look up.
  3. Ask what being wrong would look like. "If this diagnosis is wrong, what would we see in the logs?" turns a story into a prediction you can test.
  4. Run the new-hire test. Would you merge this if a new teammate sent it with no links and no tests? If not, the chat window doesn't get a pass either.
  5. Trust where you can check cheaply. In Stack Overflow's 2026 survey, 48% of developers said they trust AI when they can easily validate the answers, and only 16% extend that trust to most tasks that aren't important work decisions (2026 Developer Survey, AI section, checked November 2026). That's a sensible default: lean on AI where checking is cheap, and slow down where it isn't.

Make it a team habit

The double-charge story had two people in it, and both trusted the tone. One thing that helps is a simple review question: "Which of these claims did you check, and how?" Asked kindly and every time, it stops being an accusation and becomes part of how the team reviews.

It also helps to keep AI-written explanations out of PR descriptions unless someone has checked them. A paragraph that sounds authoritative in a PR carries the author's name, and reviewers read it as the author's own understanding. If you want a format for recording what was checked and how much checking a change needs, the post on how much testing an AI answer needs has a table and a four-line PR note.

None of this makes AI less useful. A fluent answer is often a great first draft of a hypothesis, a checklist or a fix. It's just rarely the proof.

Try this week

  • Take one AI answer you're about to act on and rewrite it as a bare list of claims. Mark the ones you've actually verified.
  • Check the most specific detail in it (a version, a flag, a function name) before anything else.
  • In your next review, ask "which claims did you check?" on a PR with an AI-written explanation.
  • Notice where you can't check an answer cheaply. Those are the places to slow down.

faqs.q: Why do fluent AI answers feel so trustworthy?
faqs.a: Easy-to-read text takes less effort, and less effort feels like agreement. With people, a clear explanation usually signals real knowledge. With language models the link is weaker: researchers from OpenAI and Georgia Tech (2025) argue that training and evaluation reward guessing over admitting uncertainty, so models often sound sure even when they are wrong.

faqs.q: Does using an AI assistant make code less secure?
faqs.a: It can. In a Stanford user study published at ACM CCS 2023 (Perry et al.), participants with an AI assistant wrote significantly less secure code than those without one, and were more likely to believe their code was secure. Participants who trusted the AI less and worked more on their prompts produced fewer vulnerabilities.

faqs.q: How do developers feel about the accuracy of AI tools?
faqs.a: In Stack Overflow's 2025 survey, 66% named "AI solutions that are almost right, but not quite" as their top frustration. In the 2026 survey, 48% said they trust AI when they can easily validate the answers, and only 16% extend that trust to most tasks that are not important work decisions.

faqs.q: What is a quick way to check a convincing AI answer?
faqs.a: Rewrite it as a short list of claims, then verify the most specific detail first: a version number, a flag, a function signature. Ask what you would expect to see if the answer were wrong, and check for that.
